If the state q and composed flux f(q) are sufficiently smooth, this integral law yields the differential conservation equation (printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2). Interesting solutions can contain discontinuities, and nonlinear conservation laws can develop them even from smooth initial data (printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2). At such a discontinuity, the differential equation does not hold classically, while the integral conservation law remains the fundamental equation that continues to hold for these solutions (printed p. 5, Section 1.1.2). The supplied passage leaves the precise solution class, endpoint conventions, and temporal interpretation of the integral balance unspecified.

Selected model [positive_dimension]: Use n = m + 1 for m a natural number, with real vector states in R^n and square real n-by-n principal matrices.

Selected model [governing_law_identity]: The governing-law data are the triple (Omega, A, b). Omega is a fixed declared set of admissible states and is part of the law, rather than an independent filter added to a law identified only by A and b. Different declared sets can therefore represent different governing-law data even when their total coefficient functions coincide.

Selected model [state_domain]: Omega may be any fixed subset of R^n. This is a classification of candidate problem data: the empty set may be stored, but it admits no Riemann problem because the two side states must belong to Omega. No openness, convexity, global integrability, or regularity of Omega is imposed.

Selected model [coordinate_domain]: Use one real spatial coordinate and one real time coordinate. The coefficient data are supplied on all R x R, and spectral hyperbolicity means at every real x and t, for every state in Omega. This chooses a global coefficient-data model; it is not a claim of solution existence for all real times or a representation theorem for arbitrary coordinate domains.

Selected model [principal_and_forcing]: A is an arbitrary supplied function R x R x R^n -> Matrix(n,n,R). b is an arbitrary supplied function R x R x R^n -> R^n. The explicit first-order equation is q_t + A(x,t,q) q_x = b(x,t,q). Nonzero forcing is permitted, with no sign, continuity, differentiability, integrability, or physical rate-law constraint. Homogeneous equations are the special case b = 0. No conservative-flux representation is required.

Selected model [spectral_condition]: For each admissible state at each real x,t, the actual matrix A(x,t,state) has a complete real eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. Eigenvalues need not be distinct; no uniform diagonalization bound, symmetrizer, or coefficient regularity is asserted.

Selected model [total_function_representation]: Lean stores total coefficient functions on the ambient state space. The governing-law domain is Omega. The residual equivalence in the target is an algebraic identity of that stored expression for arbitrary arguments; it does not impose equation solutionhood outside Omega or add a law that a solution must satisfy at every ambient state.

Selected model [problem_data]: A candidate initial-value problem consists of this governing law and an independently supplied initial state function q0 : R -> R^n. It is in the selected Riemann family exactly when the governing law satisfies the stated spectral condition and there exist left and right states in Omega with q0(x)=left for every x<0 and q0(x)=right for every x>0.

Selected model [interface_and_degeneracy]: The interface is represented at coordinate zero. The value q0(0) is wholly unspecified, including no requirement that it lie in Omega; the problem-data predicate deliberately tests only the two strict half-lines. Equal side states are admitted as a degenerate member of the two-state family. The genuine-jump subfamily additionally requires unequal side states. No quotient or equivalence of solutions under single-point changes is asserted.
